Senses.Explanation: Three teachers grant a monk only partial credit after a different exchange in each hall. Tian’an Sheng receives a monk’s successive images of the autumn wind, Yunmen’s cake, Zhaozhou’s tea, and the music of Bo Ya and Zhong Ziqi. The teacher presses him to say a word for an attuned listener, hears the monk’s answer, and says he will believe only half of it. Xiaotang finds a monk checking rice while he pulls weeds and asks whether two things are the same or different. After several challenges, the monk calls on heaven, and Xiaotang offers the same partial acceptance. At a Nirvana-day hall, Dabian Quan questions a monk about the Buddha’s birth, death, and Bodhidharma’s one sandal; when the monk offers his own formula about coming and going, the teacher again grants only half. In each scene the line recognizes some force in an answer while leaving the test unresolved.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase caps an encounter by announcing that peace now reigns after conflict or opposition falls away. Dufeng, Muchen, and Nanyue use it in distinct answers and challenges. Zhe'an closes a New Year sermon with it; Qizhen gives it after a monk's abrupt departure. Across these five uses it can voice relief, a pointed victory, or a deliberately overlarge claim of calm. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). At the transfer of ancestral tablets into a new hall, Guxue Zhenzhe asks what the old worthies discuss together. He proposes standard answers about pointing to mind, emancipation, causality, and lineage formulas, and repeats that each has no bearing on the question. He then lifts his whisk and asks whether the assembly sees. Guxue voices every retained dismissal; the repetition strips away ready-made topic labels before his concrete gesture.

Senses.Explanation: This ironic verdict says that the proposed explanation has missed the matter entirely. In the relayed Yaoshan case, the proposed explanation is dismissed with this formula; later teachers repeat it after readings of cases, inherited claims, and praise that they judge irrelevant. The prefaced 且喜 carries an ironic turn: apparent good fortune is announced while the offered account is publicly ruled to have no connection to the matter under test.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Good; the old man has understood the final word
SearchAliases: good; the old man has understood the final word
Senses.Note: After Xuefeng questions Deshan for bringing his bowl before the meal signal, Yantou privately tells Deshan something. The next day Deshan teaches differently, and Yantou claps, saying the old man has understood the final word. Yulin weighs the three elders against one another. Minshu calls their maneuvers failures, while Wansong presses what Yantou could have whispered. Linye says the exchange misled later readers; Ruibai questions Yantou’s prediction that Deshan would live only three more years. Hongzhi asks whether the final word was understood at all. The applause remains part of a contested case.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks for the phrase that brings the matter fully into view. Zhangxue Tongzui asks after saying that an earlier manner of presentation is only half; his answer pictures a chick and a dog lying by a fence in snow. Baichi Xingyuan asks at an imperial birthday sermon after saying that one phrase fully presented brings a thousand auspicious things; he moves his fly whisk and wishes peace and long life to the ruler. Eryin Mi asks after citing a warning that even a flawless world is only a turn of phrase, and answers with Maitreya in market streets and sacred presence at the writing table. Each teacher asks and answers in a different setting.

Senses.Explanation: Four teachers ask their assemblies for the vital handle of a Chan monk and answer or test the assembly in different ways. Shishuang Erzhan Zun says that even a clear display still falls within a teaching gate, then asks for the monk’s vital handle and warns against telling it to someone without wisdom. Doushuai Bulin Jian asks the same question after a sequence about Chan teaching and answers with a drum hung at Thunder Gate and a frog trying to provide the music. Shanyi Ruchun asks it after rejecting both this and not-this as final answers, replying with a turtle boring through a ruined wall and a cock crowing before dawn. Yanju Deshen asks after saying that complete nakedness still misses it; a head monk steps forward and claps, and Yanju says the monk has the handle but it remains in Yanju’s own hands. Each teacher’s question tests a present audience rather than requesting a dictionary definition.

The reply follows a present display rather than a promise to deliver a later lecture. Elsewhere in Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan, Yushan Shangsi contrasts long heavenly time with realization in one moment, then displays the whisk and describes an inexhaustible vow to help beings. Asked on what cultivation this rests, he pauses and gives the selected reply. The deferred answer redirects a demand for a verbal causal account toward the hearers' own recognition.

Senses.Explanation: An older teacher’s release of Guanxi is echoed by two later teachers in separate interviews. In an older recorded encounter, Guanxi comes to the teacher, who suddenly grips him by the chest. Guanxi says he has understood; the teacher releases him and says he will spare him one beating. At Santa, a teacher tests three visiting monks about their traveling together. After several answers, one monk asks for a compassionate way in, and the teacher says he will let one beating go; the exchange continues with the monk’s cry. At Huanglian, another teacher tests a monk on Deshan’s blows and Linji’s shouts and asks where the monk applies effort. When the monk answers that he bows to the teacher, he receives the same reprieve. The phrase is a poised release after a sharp test, not a declaration that the exchange is finished.

Senses.Explanation: Qinshan closes a difficult arrow test with this line, which receives three later applications. In the older encounter a visitor named Liang asks Qinshan about an arrow piercing three barriers. Qinshan challenges him to shoot, and when Liang hesitates, Qinshan strikes him seven times and says the line. J35 quotes this exchange before proposing a different response from Liang. J39 follows the case with a separate verse about the lord inside the pass. Yuanwu uses the same line in a different current critique of a teacher who partly lets a visitor escape. T48 quotes the original Qinshan encounter and analyzes the failed exchange in detail. The later uses do not make every source a new Qinshan scene.

Senses.Explanation: Three teachers pose a parting-sentence question in departure, retirement, and funeral settings. In a departure address, Feiyin Tongrong says that coming and going leave no fixed track and that the time to part has arrived. He asks the exact question, lays his staff across his shoulder, gives a verse about carrying it into countless peaks, and leaves the hall. Yunfu Daozhi’s retirement address begins with a staff across the shoulder and the image of leaving through a high bird path. He asks the same question and answers in the current verse with a warning to watch one’s steps. In a funeral address as the coffin of the elder Yin Zhen is raised, Gulin Zhi recounts the deceased’s service and says that his conditions of teaching are complete. He asks for the parting sentence, strikes his staff on the ground, and offers a verse likening the journey to a boat reaching the shore. In all three records the host teacher voices the question and gives the parting reply; the occasion changes what leaving means.

Senses.Explanation: Now tell me is an immediate public-interview demand for an answer or judgment, often inserted after a case, assertion, or gesture to press the audience for the next turn. Yuanwu Keqin repeatedly turns it on his assembly while raising older cases. Guanghui Lian and Wuzu Fayan use it to demand the next word; Zhaozhou Congshen presses the monastic interlocutor after his reply; Guyin Yuncong and Ying'an Tanhua use it in their own addresses. Puhua throws the demand back during his exchange with Linji Yixuan. The phrase marks the pressure to answer in each exact turn, not a resolution supplied by the dictionary.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks the assembly to account for a laugh in the scene he has just described. Hanxiu Ruqian imagines Ajnata Kaundinya in the hall laughing when he opens a convenient gate of teaching, then answers with an image of friends drunk on one cup of tea. Meixi Fudu says a lamp and pillar laugh when he offers memorial incense on his teacher’s death anniversary, and answers that they laugh at his attachment to worldly form. Shanyi Ruchun says animals and temple fixtures laugh at the Buddha’s life and Bodhidharma’s arrival, then asks why and answers with ordinary acts of dressing and eating. The one who laughs belongs to each local image.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks the assembly to account for a laugh in a scene just described. Baiyu Jingsi imagines the large-bellied figure at the gate laughing while other figures are left speechless, and asks what he laughs at. Hansong Zhicao describes Hanshan and Shide laughing amid a spring-ox image and poses the same question. Huizhou Hao asks why a village elder laughs amid a deliberately absurd procession, then answers by saying the laugh adds salt to thirst. Shanyi Ruchun imagines a stone woman laughing and clapping at a group that has become wildly self-important, then explains the laugh. The pronoun in the question points to a different figure in each address, so each answer belongs to its own scene.

Senses.Explanation: Xuedou asks what discernment Taiyuan Fu displayed in his encounter with Xuefeng, turning the old staff case toward the reader’s own judgment. Xuedou recounts Taiyuan Fu testing Xuefeng’s teaching and brings in Yunmen’s blow in a related exchange. He argues that striking many people would miss the issue, then asks what sort of eye Fu had. Lingshu Yuan follows this precise question with his own verse about the lost body of reality, a grabbed nose, and needless provocation. In the Record of Fogu’s Beat-the-Rhythm Sections, Yuanwu Keqin quotes Xuedou’s question and develops a separate answer about what Fu saw and why the ordinary appearance of an eye does not settle it. Yuejiang Zhengyin compares Fu, Xuefeng, Yunmen, and Xuedou in his own comment, then asks Xuedou a further question. The exact headword is Xuedou’s evaluative challenge, not a question uttered by Taiyuan Fu, and its specific test differs from the generic public “tell me.”

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks the assembly what truly counts as extraordinary in the immediate teaching situation. Shiqi Tongyun asks after a monk’s question and a verse about the eyes of Chan students, raises his staff, and shouts. Fogu Xingwen contrasts two elders speaking of entering and leaving the canon, says neither knows the extraordinary matter, asks the same question, and strikes with his staff before giving a verse. Hanxiu Ruqian urges his audience to accept what appears in ordinary sights and actions, then asks the question and answers after a pause with the image of a flower blooming in fire amid spring warmth. The question opens three different demonstrations rather than naming a single marvel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪霽辭去。地藏門送之。問云。上座尋常說三界唯心。萬法唯識。乃指庭下片石云。且道。此石在心內在心外。師云。在心內。地藏云。行脚人。著甚麼來由安片石在心頭。師窘無以對。即放包依席下。求決擇。近一月餘。日呈見解說道理。地藏語之云。佛法不恁麼。師云。某甲詞窮理絕也。地藏云。若論佛法。一切見成。師於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1991.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wenyi of Qingliang Monastery, Jinling. As Fayan Wenyi prepares to leave after a snowbound visit, Luohan Guichen accompanies him to the gate. Luohan recalls Fayan's habitual claim that the three realms are only mind and all things only consciousness. Pointing to a stone in the courtyard, he asks whether this stone is inside or outside mind. Fayan answers that it is inside. Why, Luohan asks, should a traveling practitioner place a stone upon his mind? Unable to answer, Fayan puts down his pack and stays to seek resolution. For more than a month he presents interpretations, which Luohan rejects; only when Fayan says his words and reasons are exhausted does Luohan say that everything is already present, and the record reports Fayan's awakening. The headword turns a broad doctrinal claim into a concrete test. Neither the first reply nor a later corrected spatial answer is certified as its resolution.

Occurrences.Kwic: 藏又問：「上座尋常說三界唯心，萬法唯識。」乃指庭石曰：「且道此石在心內？在心外？」眼曰：「心內。」藏曰：「行腳人著什來繇，安片石在心頭？」眼窘求住，藏曰：「若論佛法，一切現成。」法眼于是大悟。所以道：「會得聲色問處，透聲色也不難；識得凳子來繇，周匝有餘都了。」慧超咨和尚：「如何是佛？」曰：「汝是慧超。」僧問：「如何是曹源一滴水？」曰：「是曹源一滴水。」正是：山河在我眼裏，自己只在目前。鳥啼花落水茫茫，月白風清山楚楚。說甚唯心唯識，豈關句裏言前？六相義，金絡索挂來；四法界，玉連環拋出。總是弄猢猻圈子，祭鬼神茶飯。何用將心湊泊，頭頭釘釘膠黏？不如信手拈來，處處箭鋒相拄。以致永明博綜于《宗鏡》，座主彷彿于言詮。此祖宗妙極而流弊，痛挽之，惟望後人之實證也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB299.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Sanfeng Zang. Hanyue Fazang, also called Sanfeng, raises Luohan's stone question and Fayan's inability to answer the rebuke. He then relates Fayan's later reply to Huichao's question about Buddha: 'You are Huichao.' His own verse sets mountains and rivers within his eyes and himself directly before him, with birdsong, falling flowers, water, moon and wind. Why speak of mind-only or consciousness-only, he asks, or look for the matter before or within sentences? He calls the resulting doctrinal formulas hoops for performing monkeys and food offered to ghosts, rejecting the habit of fastening mind to every word like glue. Instead he urges a freely taken response that meets each occasion point to point, and looks to later practitioners for actual realization. The exact stone question remains Luohan's quoted voice. Sanfeng's present criticism does not choose 'outside' as the missing correct answer; it challenges the mode of verbal attachment exposed by the old exchange.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks listeners to find the snag in the case or claim just presented. Xiaotang comments that Guishan’s response to Yangshan leaves the matter unsettled, then asks where the confusion lies and invites those with eyes to discern it. Yunwai Xingze asks after saying delusion and awakening both occur in the same wisdom, then waves his fly whisk and offers a verse. Xianglin Benzhen recounts Nanquan breaking a pot after a cook’s answer, asks where the snag lies, and follows with an image of playing a flute before tapping the incense table. These are three current teachers’ questions about different cases; none is a line spoken by the old figures inside the cases.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks the assembly how to respond at the decisive point after setting up a particular problem. Yuan’an Liao criticizes seeking awakening in sights and sounds, then asks the question and answers after a pause by opening his fly whisk and pointing toward the hills. Huizhou Hao says that calling a thing the true person mistakes a thief for a son, while denying it abandons one’s father; he asks what to do and replies with the image of a goose separating milk from water. Hongzhi Zhengjue asks the question after warning that clever handling cannot be shifted or bargained over, then points to a measure and weight. Yuanwu Keqin asks it while commenting on a case about the rhinoceros, inviting listeners to take up the unresolved question themselves. The exact words recur, but each teacher has prepared a different situation for the challenge.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher challenges the assembly to name an object after unsettling available names. Faxi Yin asks at a Guanyin hall after saying that calling the image an ancient Buddha or Guanyin leads back to the other name, and he bows. Nouyun Zhenshi asks in a Buddha hall after saying that calling the image Buddha would be his fault while refusing that name would miss what is before them; he strikes his staff and gives an image of a one-horned auspicious creature. Zisu Chaoyuan raises a staff after a monk’s question and asks what to call it when familiar labels and a verse about not changing with the seasons both fail. The local objects differ, while each question presses the act of naming.

Senses.Explanation: After offering his own response to an old case, a teacher asks the assembly to judge how far his answer stands from the earlier teacher’s. The clause is a direct challenge to compare a present response with an older one, and its force depends on the case each speaker has just revised. Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts Tong’an’s elaborate house-style replies with his own cloud-tilling, rain-sowing, coarse-tea answers. Feiyin Tongrong quotes an old reply about winter and offers cold wind instead before asking the comparison question and leaving the seat. Yongji Rong cites an old claim of being the same age as empty space, gives his own older-brother answer, then asks how far apart the answers are. Lianyue Daozheng criticizes an earlier New Year exchange for trapping people in existence and nonexistence, offers an alternative blessing for the emperor, and turns the same comparison back on his listeners. The exact phrase is each current teacher’s evaluative challenge, not a line spoken by the old figures.

Senses.Explanation: Four teachers pose the same challenge and answer it with different images. In a Wumen Huikai discourse, dragons and tigers furnish an extravagant display, yet the teacher says it has no bearing on a Chan monk. He asks what strength such a monk has, raises his whisk and answers with a sword reaching to the sky. A second recorded teacher asks the question after a discussion of mind and teaching, then answers with an image of a war horse whose service has gone unrecognized. A third contrasts the deaths of earlier teachers before asking the question and replying with a donkey at one house and a horse at another. A fourth retells Nanquan and the water buffalo, then asks the question and turns to a verse about the passing days of the year. The question is a challenge in four separate discourses, with no common answer attached to it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB387.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gusuzun. Gusu asks who knows gratitude after a verse on obligation, then strikes the Chan seat.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher asks who actually recognizes and repays what has been received. Tianyin Yuanxiu asks after a verse about repaying kindness and then says that the usual marks of spiritual attainment do not yet make one skilled in gratitude. Baiyu Jingsi asks after speaking of transmitting the Buddha’s seal and of teachers who seemed to oppose their predecessors, then points to an elder. Gusu Zun asks after a verse on obligation, pauses, strikes the Chan seat with a ruyi, and calls the exchange a poor bargain. Each teacher uses the same question to test gratitude in a different relation.

Senses.Explanation: Four teachers ask where the way ahead lies and answer through gestures or situational images. Fushi Tongxian asks the question after lines about paths reaching everywhere and follows it with a forceful shout. Gulin Jiru asks it while placing relics in a tower and answers with flowing water and a cloud returning to its cave. Hanxiu Ruqian asks it after a verse about the hidden pass, then strikes the Chan seat with his fly whisk. Lianfeng Su asks it while raising the torch at a funeral and tells the listeners to recognize the way directly. The question does not have one fixed direction: each teacher makes the roadhead immediate in a separate present act.

Entries.SourceTerm: 且隨老木同寒瘠，將逐春風入燒瘢

Senses.PreferredTarget: For now stay with the old tree in its cold bareness; then follow the spring wind into scorched ground
AlternateTargets: Share the old tree’s winter sparseness for a while, and in spring move into the burned patch with the wind
SearchAliases: old tree cold bareness spring wind scorched ground Zen
Hongzhi old tree spring wind burned patch
Senses.Note: Hongzhi closes a verse on Dongshan’s no-grass question by pairing an old tree’s cold sparseness with a later move into scorched ground on the spring wind. Ruibai and Hanxiu use this contrast after asking whether to hold fast or let movement proceed. Yun’e gives the pair after Yunmen’s bare-tree answer, then says each side has a cost. The two scenes test how one shifts between restraint and release without making either a permanent resting place.

Occurrences.Kwic: 下覓醫人，將閻羅王腳跟一艾爝，大唐天子通身慶快。會麼？今日是俞居士同令堂及眾夫人設齋，請山僧陞座說法，為大眾結般若緣。且道如何是般若？」良久云：「黃牛頭上兩個角，草鞋肚裏四條觔。」僧問：「千尺寒松秀，金鸞石鳳啼。是何意旨？」師云：「石傘峰頭傳消息。」進云：「是阿誰的境界？」師云：「五雲溪畔長冰花。」僧拜。上堂。「飄零黃葉，傳古佛之家風；游衍行雲，顯當人之面目。稽山寂寂，西來大意全彰；爐嶽巍巍，列祖真機獨露。戒珠閃爍，慧鏡常明。一道神光，貫徹今古。會麼？覓火和煙得，擔泉帶月歸。今日是邢吉先居士設齋，為山僧慶誕，請陞座說法，為大眾結般若緣。即此以祈居士智門了辦，道果圓成。大眾！且道圓成一句作麼生舉揚？」良久云：「轉功就位琴堂冷，退位朝君古殿寒。」便下座。解制上堂。「把住也，結定布袋口，封住拄杖頭，鐵壁銀山，鳥不飛度，直至三江浪息，大地波沉；放行也，陽和氣轉，遍界春回，直得枯木生花，冰河發焰。正當恁麼時，還放行好？把住好。」良久云：「且隨老木同寒瘠，將逐春風入燒瘢。莫有逞驢唇馬嘴者？出來吃棒。」僧問：「把住放行即不問，當體無依事若何？」師云：「今朝臘月八。」僧拂袖云：「恁麼無掛礙，隨處逞風流。」師云：「三十棒。」進云：「凍雲飛盡孤輪迥，徹底無私遍界輝。」師豎拂云：「跳不出這一重。」僧喝，禮拜，師呵呵大笑，下座。上堂。湖城錢夫人設齋，請師陞座。云：「三春已過韶華老，李白桃紅何處討？菜花滿地黃如金，燕子梁間指示人。」遂豎拂云：「會麼？於此會得，頭頭釋迦出世；於此不會，步步彌勒下生。」良久云：「鳥啼花發笑，雲興宇宙清。今日是湖城錢開府老夫人及眾比丘尼送法衣上山，設齋修福延生，請山僧陞座，為眾結般若緣。且道般若一句如何舉揚？夏初日漸暖，行人盡解襟。」後堂素朴問：「高提祖印，最上一乘，弘範毘尼，一乘最上。今日和尚二法並談，施主功德還有邊際也無？」師云：「弁石播苔痕。」進云：「青龍峰頂獅子吼，百千群品證無生。」便禮拜。師云：「非為分外。」遂下座。上堂。崇禎甲戌年十月望日，龍華結制。唐孝廉祈遠居士，請師陞座。拈香畢，乃云：「世尊初成道日云：『奇哉！眾生皆具如來智慧德相。』儒書亦云：『在明明德。』《康誥》曰：『克明德。』《太甲》曰：『顧諟天之明命。』昨夜青龍崗起舞，花石澗𨁝跳，驚得獅子巖，向象王峰鼻
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB188.xml). Recorded sayings. Ruibai contrasts holding fast with allowing movement, then voices Hongzhi’s closing pair as his present answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上誕生現瑞，是汝諸人還見麼？」復卓一卓，云：「將正法眼藏涅槃妙心實相無相秘密法門直截吐露了也。還聞麼？如其見處分明、聞處透脫，便能塞乎天地、耀古騰今；脫或未然。」乃擲下拄杖，云：「大眾普同到佛殿上香念誦。」中秋日，過霍丘福昌寺，眾請陞座。「平白地上拈起一絲毫頭，盡大地人亡鋒結舌，未審利害在甚麼處？眾中莫有知委者麼？不妨出來道看。」僧問：「日往月來即不問，中秋佳節時如何？」師云：「當軒月正圓。」進云：「恁麼則人人且慶中秋節，家家齊唱太平歌。」師云：「切忌瞻望。」僧擬議，師云：「這鈍漢。」僧禮拜，師乃云：「秋風清，秋月明，秋雲淡蕩，秋水澄渟，歷祖示為向上巴鼻，諸佛演作妙淨明心，山僧直截指似，未審諸人惺不惺？急薦取，莫沉吟，庭前秋色數株翠，額上眉毛八字橫。」復舉：「僧問雲門禪師云：『樹彫葉落時如何？』門云：『體露金風。』」師云：「雲門老漢雖則手親眼辨，善赴來機；仔細簡點將來，猶欠一著在。山僧今日忽有問：『樹彫葉落時如何？』只向伊道：『且隨老木同寒瘠，將逐春風入燒瘢。』此語有兩負門，具眼者試辨看。」擊拂子，下座。福昌大眾請師開示。「若論斯事，人人具足、箇箇圓明，本無遮障之緣，豈假開示之說？蓋為多生以來不覺一念妄動，逐於諸塵蕩而忘返，故有生死苦海輪迴不息耳。即今也無別等玄妙奇特所示，只要汝諸人向二六時中、四威儀處回光返照，於一念未生已前忽然知歸，方解念起而無所起、眼見而無所見、耳聞而無所聞、心思而無所思，便爾頭頭不昧、剎剎圓融。山僧如此告報，是汝諸人直下還會麼？若不會，歸堂喫茶處薦得，方信不吾欺也。」晚參。舉：「南泉示眾云：『王老師自小養一頭水牯牛，擬向谿東牧，未免犯他國王水艸；擬向谿西牧，亦未免犯他國王水艸。不如隨分納些些，總不見得。』」師云：「南泉老漢大似掩鼻偷香，不顧傍觀者哂。何故聻？夾路桃花風雨後，馬蹄無處避殘紅。」上堂。「當頭拈出，充塞十虛；直下知歸，了無一事。即此打破生死牢關，隨緣得用；掀翻識情窠臼，徹見根源。不唯歷歷明明，更是綿綿密密。所以道：乾坤廓落無邊表，杲日當天宇宙明。」赴光山請，謝別眾緇素，上堂。「玄機普應，妙密無方，充滿十虛，貫通三際。所以道：無邊剎境，自他不隔於毫端；十世古今，始終不離於當念。然則衲僧境界，信意安排，是處家山而元無彼此，隨緣自在而何妨去來？客秋到

Occurrences.Kwic: 也。」僧禮拜。乃云：「杲日當天，光輝萬象，璿璣運轉天關，金鰲統該地軸。空中木馬，長淅瀝以嘶風；海底泥牛，時滂湃以駕浪。吞月蝦蟆居井底，抱兒石虎臥岩前。於斯明得向上一路別有家風，格外提持，靈機迥異。且作麼是向上一路？還委悉麼？古殿西風寒颯颯，一聲鴻唯過遼天。」解制，上堂。僧問：「師未陞座時，還有佛法也無？」師云：「有。」進云：「如何是未陞座時佛法？」師云：「高低古柏沿山翠，長短幽篁滿澗青。」進云：「陞座後又如何？」師云：「一片白雲橫谷口，幾多歸鳥自迷巢。」問：「學人得得到五臺，因甚麼不見文殊？」師云：「望嵩樓畔陽人聚。」進云：「學人不會，請師直指。」師云：「此去汝州不遠。」僧禮拜。乃云：「一向把住，今日放行。其把住也，壁立萬仞，水泄不通，白雲寺裏高掛缽囊，眉毛廝結，一箇箇掃蹤絕跡，直至千江浪息，大地平沉；其放行也，陽和氣轉，暖律初回，風穴山中橫擔拄杖，緊峭草鞋，一箇箇放光動地，只得冰河發燄，枯木生花。正恁麼時，還是把住好？放行好？且隨老木同寒瘠，將逐春風入燒瘢。」金粟虎堂和尚專使至，請上堂。僧問：「世尊雪山睹明星大悟，又悟箇甚麼？」師云：「鼻孔大頭垂。」進云：「分明成現事，何用受辛勤？」師云：「若不如是，焉知如是？」進云：「只如殃崛救產，還是佛法靈驗？還是果熟自落？」師云：「佛法靈驗，果熟自落。」進云：「古人不見今時月，今月曾經照古人。」師云：「引不著。」僧禮拜，師云：「切忌躲跟。」乃云：「連枝同氣，共闡向上宗猷；正令全提，各自隨機應變。灑汝海之一雨，萬卉欣榮；繼金粟之遺蹤，真燈昺耀。光揚先師法道，提獎後進弟昆，在吾金粟虎兄堂頭和尚矣，不任歡慶。似僕無識之夫，謬主斯席，恒愧素餐，何期實念松麓二上座遠從金粟、深入白雲，得得遠馳書幣來此設齋，仍請陞座為眾舉揚向上宗乘，過沐周勤，仰荷不已，風穴只得應時擊節，為諸人舉揚去也。」遂驀豎拂子，召大眾云：「看看，沼祖來也。在風穴拂子頭上道：『祖師心印，狀似鐵牛之機，去即印住，住即印破，向上牢關，急須照顧，眼孔定動，早已蹉過。』遂震威一喝。」復舉：「僧問古德云：『深山中還有佛法也無？』德云：『有。』僧云：『如何是深山裏佛法？』德云：『石頭大底大，小底小。』」師云：「風穴又則不然，今日若有人問：『如何是深山裏佛法？』只向道：『衝開碧落松千尺，截斷紅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB383.xml). Recorded sayings. Hanxiu likewise contrasts holding fast with allowing movement and gives the pair as a current response.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a slap across the cheek
AlternateTargets: a sharp slap to the face
SearchAliases: a sharp slap to the face
Senses.Explanation: Tianyin Yuanxiu raises an encounter in which the deity Shengsi says he has never seen the non-retreating deity in this Buddha-land, and the latter replies that he too has not been seen there. If they have never met, Tianyin asks, how are they face to face now? He would answer as the non-retreating deity with a slap across the cheek; taking the other role, he would spit in the other's face. These imagined interventions prevent the present encounter from being missed beneath the claims of non-meeting. The exact slap is Tianyin's proposed action, not an assault reported in the inherited meeting. Huigong Kaixiong comments on Lingyin Wentai meeting Xueting Fuyu. Asked to give the sentence fitting the moment, Lingyin is about to speak when Xueting says his property has been confiscated and he is still complaining. Lingyin claps, protests and eventually bows. Huigong says that at the first question Lingyin should have given a slap across the cheek; even lightning-fast response would then leave the old master unable to recover. His cap criticizes failure to act decisively and calls the final bow a dead snake spitting poison. The slap is a counterfactual alternative proposed by Huigong, not an action the quoted dialogue records. Hansong Zhicao raises a monk asking Qinglong Miaopu why he does not bow to the Buddha. Qinglong slaps him, asks if he understands, and answers his failure to understand with 'The household has no two masters.' Hansong praises the great capacity of the action but also compares claiming sovereignty where no Buddha is present to an old woman selling wine. His own verse says that asking why he does not bow abandons a pearl to seek a treasure, and that the slap knocks the whole person over. The exact phrase is Hansong's verse description of Qinglong's action; its praise remains qualified by the following regret at the final words. On receiving his late teacher's final letter, Yuejiang Zhengyin offers incense and pictures a violent wind overturning the foremost peak. To say the teacher has died wrongs heaven; to say he has not died also wrongs heaven. A slap across the cheek and three punches under the ribs follow, then Yuejiang recalls the matter privately and regrets not settling that grievance earlier. The blows are forceful memorial language inside the incense address. The source does not identify an actual recipient struck then, and the contradictory claims about death should not be smoothed into an unqualified declaration of physical immortality.
Senses.Note: The local challenge and the current teacher's response govern the reading; quoted evaluations are not universal factual claims.

The exact phrase is Hansong's verse description of Qinglong's action; its praise remains qualified by the following regret at the final words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若謂先師不滅度，蒼天苦屈。攔腮一掌，肋下三拳，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1409.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuejiang Zhengyin. On receiving his late teacher's final letter, Yuejiang Zhengyin offers incense and pictures a violent wind overturning the foremost peak. To say the teacher has died wrongs heaven; to say he has not died also wrongs heaven. A slap across the cheek and three punches under the ribs follow, then Yuejiang recalls the matter privately and regrets not settling that grievance earlier. The blows are forceful memorial language inside the incense address. The source does not identify an actual recipient struck then, and the contradictory claims about death should not be smoothed into an unqualified declaration of physical immortality.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂舉拂子云昔日世尊拈花迦葉微笑今夜㱕宗舉拂大眾寂然為復寂然者是微笑者是又是箇什麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters. At a farewell evening talk at Jiufeng in Junzhou, the present Guizong record master raises his whisk before the assembly. He recalls the story in which the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kasyapa smiled, then contrasts that response with the assembly's silence before his own raised whisk. He asks whether silence or smiling is the point and whether the whisk and flower are the same or different. He then gives a verse on returning to the source and responding flexibly. The Buddha is the historical figure in the story; the Guizong master is the current speaker using it to test his listeners.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The direct-turn frame marks the present Guizong record master raising the whisk and speaking. He recalls the Buddha and Kasyapa inside his own utterance; the historical actors are not the current speaker.

Senses.Explanation: The Guizong master invokes the Buddha's flower gesture while raising his own whisk before a silent assembly. In this farewell evening talk, he recalls Kasyapa smiling at the Buddha's flower, then asks whether the assembly's silence or the old smile is the response and whether his whisk is the same as the flower. His closing verse directs listeners to respond flexibly instead of fixing the demonstration as identical or different.

Senses.Explanation: The question tests whether Pang can present to another person the phrase that proved effective for him at Nanyue. In the road encounter, Pang says he has shared it and points to himself when Bailing asks with whom. Bailing praises him, but Pang then asks who could know the phrase, and Bailing puts on his hat and leaves. Four recorded teachers cite this one older conversation and answer it differently: Miyun says Bailing would have no way out without Dahui, Jie’an Jin compares the two participants and lifts his staff, Pofeng Chong praises Pang’s handling of danger, and Heyizi dismisses the whole chain of appraisals. The exact question remains Bailing’s old utterance throughout.

Senses.Explanation: “Purely one, without admixture” appraises continuous activity with nothing mixed into it. Senses.Explanation: Utterly clear, without a speck names a state of apparent purity that Chan speakers often put to a further test. Poshan asks whether his address is spotless or muddy. Liangting grants the speckless state but says the person in the snow house can still be lost. Hanyue describes people aiming for a perfectly pure, undisturbed state while criticizing what they take as the goal. Jingting says even exposing constancy has not reached spotless clarity. Wuyi warns against sitting contentedly in pure stillness and losing the thread of inquiry. Xueyan calls the speckless point a continuing flow, then points to eating and tea. Gaofeng recounts a period of pure, uninterrupted stillness before a later event shattered his earlier understanding.

Senses.Explanation: To put understanding to immediate use in the midst of one's ongoing practice, commonly opposed to letting it circulate at the level of conventional discourse. Guizong Zhichang explicitly contrasts understanding, which permits use on the way, with failure to understand, which leaves conventional circulation. Yuanwu Keqin compares such use to a dragon gaining water and a tiger leaning on a mountain. Zhenjing Kewen says that understanding yields use on the way and then asks what transmission would be if it were not such use. Jingzhao warns beginners to return to the source and not seek use on the way, showing the phrase can name a tempting pragmatic appropriation rather than an unconditional good.
